blocks.text: The ophthalmoscope is an instrument used to examine the interior of the eye, particularly the retina, optic disc, retinal blood vessels and macula. It is an essential instrument in general medicine, pediatrics, emergency medicine, ophthalmology and clinical OSCE examinations.
The aim of this guide is to help you identify the instrument, explain its clinical applications, demonstrate the examination correctly, interpret findings and answer follow-up questions confidently.
Name: Ophthalmoscope.
Classification: Diagnostic instrument used for ocular examination.
Main types:
A. Direct ophthalmoscope
Produces an upright, virtual image with relatively high magnification, typically about 15×. It provides a small field of view and is commonly used during routine bedside examinations.
B. Indirect ophthalmoscope

Usually consists of a light source mounted on a headset and a separate condensing lens. It produces a real, inverted and laterally reversed image, provides a wider field of view and is particularly useful for examining the peripheral retina.
C. Panoptic or wide-field direct ophthalmoscope
A modified handheld design that provides a wider view of the fundus than a conventional direct ophthalmoscope.
OSCE identification statement:

“This is an ophthalmoscope, a diagnostic instrument used to examine the fundus of the eye, including the optic disc, retina, retinal vessels and macula. The handheld direct ophthalmoscope is commonly used for bedside examination.”
The ophthalmoscope helps identify ocular abnormalities and signs of systemic disease.

rows: Swelling of the optic disc, potentially associated with raised intracranial pressure
Arteriolar narrowing, arteriovenous crossing changes and retinal haemorrhages
Optic disc pallor, swelling and other abnormalities
Vessel occlusion, haemorrhages and other vascular changes
Possible retinal or optic nerve causes of visual disturbance
Fundus assessment when clinically indicated, including assessment for papilloedema
Selected retinal, optic nerve and red-reflex abnormalities

blocks.text: Important: A normal direct ophthalmoscopic examination does not exclude serious eye disease or raised intracranial pressure.

blocks.text: Large and small spots
The large spot is useful for routine fundus examination; the small spot is helpful through smaller pupils or when examining infants.
Red-free filter
A green filter that improves the visibility of retinal blood vessels and certain haemorrhages.
Special apertures
Slit, fixation target or other patterns may be available depending on the model. Their functions vary by manufacturer.

items.text: Portable and easy to carry during ward rounds.
Relatively inexpensive compared with many specialist ophthalmic devices.
Provides high magnification of the optic disc and central retina.
Does not usually require a separate condensing lens.
Useful for bedside examinations and rapid clinical assessment.
Can be used in children, including neonates, when an appropriate technique and aperture are selected.
Can reveal important systemic disease manifestations in the retina.
Small field of view: only a limited portion of the fundus is visible at a time.
Limited peripheral retinal assessment: peripheral tears and lesions may be missed.
Pupil dependence: a small pupil can make examination difficult.
Media opacity: cataracts, corneal opacity or vitreous haemorrhage may obstruct the view.
Operator dependence: correct alignment, focusing and interpretation require practice.
Accommodation and refractive error: the examiner's and patient's refractive states can affect focus.
Limited stereoscopic assessment: conventional direct ophthalmoscopy generally provides little or no useful stereopsis compared with binocular indirect examination.
Not a complete eye examination: it does not replace visual acuity testing, slit-lamp examination, tonometry or specialist retinal assessment when indicated.

blocks.text: Examiner tip: If asked why an indirect ophthalmoscope is preferred for examining the peripheral retina, answer that it offers a wider field of view and can be used with techniques that provide a more comprehensive peripheral retinal examination.
Before starting, explain the procedure and obtain consent.

items.text: Ophthalmoscope is clean and functioning.
Battery is charged or the power source is working.
Light intensity is appropriate.
Lens wheel and aperture selector work.
The patient's glasses or contact lenses are addressed as appropriate.
The room can be dimmed.
The patient is seated comfortably, or appropriately positioned if an infant.
Relevant history is obtained, including eye pain, trauma, visual changes and relevant eye disease.
Ask about photophobia, painful red eye, recent eye trauma and previous eye surgery.
Use an appropriate brightness, particularly in infants and children.
Avoid prolonged, unnecessarily intense illumination.
Clean the instrument according to the manufacturer's instructions and local infection-control policy.
Do not touch the patient's eye with the instrument.
Do not instil dilating drops unless appropriately indicated, prescribed or authorised, and after relevant contraindications and precautions have been considered.

blocks.text: Pupil dilation: Mydriatic drops can improve the view, but they are not always necessary. They may cause temporary blurred near vision and photophobia, and can precipitate acute angle-closure glaucoma in susceptible eyes. In emergencies, the decision to dilate must not delay urgent assessment or management.

subsections.subsection_title: 7. How to use a direct ophthalmoscope — step-by-step OSCE demonstration

blocks.text: “Hello, I am going to examine the back of your eyes using an ophthalmoscope. I will shine a light into each eye. It may be bright, but the examination should not be painful. Is that alright?”
Confirm the patient's identity, obtain consent, wash your hands and position the patient comfortably.

content_groups.group_title: Step 2: Prepare the room and instrument

blocks.text: Dim the room lights. Switch on the ophthalmoscope, select a suitable aperture and choose a comfortable brightness.
For a routine adult examination, a large round aperture is often appropriate. Use a smaller aperture when necessary, such as with a small pupil.
Ask the patient to look at a distant target. From approximately 30–50 cm away, shine the light through the pupil and look for the red-orange reflex.

items.text: A uniform reflex is generally reassuring.
An absent, diminished or asymmetric reflex requires further assessment.
A white reflex, or leukocoria, is abnormal and requires urgent ophthalmic evaluation, especially in a child.

blocks.text: For the patient's right eye, use your right eye and hold the ophthalmoscope in your right hand. For the patient's left eye, use your left eye and left hand.
Approach from approximately 15 degrees temporal to the patient's line of sight. Keep the other eye open where practical.
Ask the patient to look at a distant target. From a distance of roughly 30–45 cm, direct the light through the pupil, then move closer while maintaining alignment.
Follow the retinal vessels toward their origin to help locate the optic disc if necessary.
Turn the diopter wheel until the structures appear clear.

items.text: Negative lenses generally help focus on a more myopic optical system.
Positive lenses generally help focus on a more hyperopic optical system.

blocks.text: The exact setting depends on the patient's and examiner's refractive states, accommodation and the instrument.
A. Optic disc
Assess colour, margins, cup-to-disc ratio, symmetry and swelling.
B. Retinal vessels
Assess calibre, branching, arteriovenous crossing changes, haemorrhages and exudates.
C. Macula
Ask the patient to look directly at the light briefly when assessing the macula, as tolerated. Examine for pigmentary changes, exudates and other lesions.
D. Retina
Examine the visible posterior retina for haemorrhages, exudates, lesions and abnormalities. Remember that the direct ophthalmoscope does not adequately exclude peripheral retinal disease.
Repeat the examination using the opposite hand and eye. Compare both sides for asymmetry.
Thank the patient, switch off the instrument, clean it as required and wash your hands. Explain your findings and document any abnormalities.
Red reflex → Optic disc → Vessels → Retina → Macula → Other eye.
The examiner may expect a broader ocular examination too, including visual acuity, pupils and visual fields, depending on the station instructions.
An ophthalmoscope is a non-invasive diagnostic instrument. There are no absolute contraindications to routine ophthalmoscopy itself in most patients.

items.text: Using an ophthalmoscope: usually safe and non-invasive.
Dilating the pupil: introduces additional drug-related risks and requires clinical judgement.
Suspected open-globe injury: avoid pressure on the eye and do not delay emergency referral for a routine examination.

blocks.text: This is one of the most important sections for OSCEs because the examiner may show you a fundus photograph or ask you to describe your findings.
A. Normal optic disc

items.text: Pink or orange-pink.
Distinct, well-defined margins.
Central physiological cup.
No pathological swelling or pallor.

blocks.text: B. Papilloedema

items.text: Swollen optic disc with blurred margins.
Venous congestion may be present.
Haemorrhages may occur.

blocks.text: Significance: may indicate raised intracranial pressure and requires urgent evaluation. A normal fundus does not exclude raised intracranial pressure.
C. Diabetic retinopathy

items.text: Microaneurysms.
Dot-blot haemorrhages.
Hard exudates.
Cotton-wool spots in some cases.
Neovascularisation in proliferative disease.

blocks.text: Significance: suggests diabetic retinal microvascular disease; grading requires an appropriate retinal examination.
D. Hypertensive retinopathy

items.text: Generalised or focal arteriolar narrowing.
Arteriovenous crossing changes.
Retinal haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots in more severe disease.
Optic disc swelling may occur in a severe hypertensive emergency.

blocks.text: Significance: interpret with the blood pressure and overall clinical condition.
E. Optic atrophy

items.text: Abnormally pale optic disc.
May be associated with reduced visual acuity, colour vision or visual fields.

blocks.text: Significance: suggests optic nerve damage from various causes.
F. Leukocoria

items.text: White rather than the expected red-orange pupillary reflex.

blocks.text: Significance: requires urgent assessment to exclude serious conditions, including retinoblastoma and congenital cataract.

content_groups.group_title: How to describe the fundus in an examination

items.text: Red reflex: present, absent, diminished or abnormal.
Optic disc: colour, margins, swelling and cup-to-disc ratio.
Retinal vessels: calibre, pattern and abnormalities.
Retina: haemorrhages, exudates, lesions or other changes.
Macula: appearance and visible abnormalities.
Comparison: whether findings are symmetrical between the eyes.

blocks.text: Model normal finding:

“The red reflex is present bilaterally. Both optic discs appear pink with well-defined margins and no visible swelling. The retinal vessels have a normal appearance, and no obvious retinal haemorrhages or exudates are seen. The visible maculae appear unremarkable.”
Only report structures you have actually visualised. If the view is inadequate, document that the fundus could not be adequately assessed rather than calling it normal.
Ophthalmoscopy in children requires a gentle approach, appropriate positioning and attention to developmental differences.

items.text: Use an appropriately sized aperture and a comfortable light intensity.
Examine the red reflex in both eyes.
A parent or caregiver may help comfort and position the child.
Consider congenital cataract, retinoblastoma and other causes of an abnormal red reflex.
Preterm infants require retinal screening according to established retinopathy of prematurity protocols; a handheld direct ophthalmoscope is not a substitute for the required specialist examination.
Explain the procedure using age-appropriate language.
Ask the child to look at a distant object.
Keep the examination brief and allow breaks.
Examine the red reflex and fundus where clinically indicated.
Use distraction and caregiver reassurance to improve cooperation.

blocks.text: An abnormal, absent, asymmetric or white reflex warrants prompt assessment. Do not assume that a normal external eye appearance excludes significant intraocular disease.

items.text: Avoid unnecessarily prolonged or intense illumination.
Do not force a struggling child into a position that could cause injury.
Do not delay urgent referral while repeatedly attempting an inadequate examination.
Pupil dilation in children should follow an appropriate clinical protocol.

subsections.subsection_title: 12. Common OSCE questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is an ophthalmoscope used for?
Answer: It is used to examine the fundus of the eye, particularly the optic disc, retina, retinal vessels and macula.
Q2. What is the difference between direct and indirect ophthalmoscopy?

Answer: Direct ophthalmoscopy provides a highly magnified, upright virtual image with a small field of view. Indirect ophthalmoscopy provides an inverted image with a wider field of view and is better suited to examining the peripheral retina.
Q3. Why do you examine the red reflex?
Answer: To assess the optical pathway through the ocular media and identify abnormalities such as cataract, other media opacities or leukocoria.
Q4. What are the features of a normal optic disc?
Answer: It is generally pink or orange-pink, with distinct margins and a physiological cup. There should be no pathological swelling or abnormal pallor.
Q5. What is papilloedema?
Answer: Papilloedema is optic disc swelling caused by raised intracranial pressure. It requires urgent clinical assessment because the underlying cause may be serious.
Q6. What is the cup-to-disc ratio?

Answer: It is the ratio of the diameter of the optic cup to the overall diameter of the optic disc. An increased ratio or asymmetry may suggest glaucoma, but interpretation depends on disc size, clinical findings and other investigations.
Q7. Why do you use your right hand and right eye for the patient's right eye?
Answer: It allows the examiner to approach from the temporal side while minimising interference from the patient's nose and reducing face-to-face contact.
Q8. Why should the patient look at a distant target?
Answer: It helps maintain fixation and reduces accommodation, making the examination easier.
Q9. What causes a white pupillary reflex in a child?
Answer: Causes include retinoblastoma, congenital cataract and other intraocular abnormalities. It requires urgent ophthalmic assessment.
Q10. What are the limitations of direct ophthalmoscopy?
Answer: It has a narrow field of view, provides limited peripheral retinal assessment, may be difficult through small pupils or opaque media, and is operator-dependent.
Q11. Can a normal ophthalmoscopic examination exclude raised intracranial pressure?
Answer: No. Papilloedema may be absent, particularly early in the disease. Clinical assessment and appropriate investigations remain essential.
Q12. What is the significance of retinal haemorrhages and exudates?

Answer: They may occur in diabetic retinopathy, hypertensive retinopathy, retinal vascular disorders and other conditions. Their distribution and associated findings help establish the differential diagnosis.
Mistake: Using the wrong eye and hand
Correction: Use your right eye and hand for the patient's right eye, and your left eye and hand for the patient's left eye.
Mistake: Starting too close to the patient
Correction: Begin at a distance to assess the red reflex, then approach while maintaining alignment.
Mistake: Forgetting the red reflex
Correction: Assess it before attempting detailed fundus examination, particularly in children.
Mistake: Examining only the optic disc
Correction: Examine the vessels, visible retina and macula as well, and compare both eyes.
Mistake: Using excessive light
Correction: Use the lowest comfortable brightness that provides an adequate view, particularly in children.
Examiner tip: Narrate your technique
State what you are assessing, maintain patient comfort, and describe the findings systematically. If the view is poor, acknowledge the limitation and explain the next step.

Raised intracranial pressure

Macula, external ear, red reflex, optic disc

blocks.text: The key principle: Do not simply name the ophthalmoscope. Demonstrate safe technique, describe the fundus systematically, recognise urgent abnormalities and explain the limitations of your findings.
